3.7.1.officialText: use standard notations for vectors, i.e. f p , x i + y j , f p y , x i + y j + z k , AB , a
3.7.1.spineTitleVerbatim: use standard notations for vectors, i.e. f p , x i + y j , f p y , x i + y j + z k , AB , a

resources.title: Hit the spot
resources.evidence: The task has students 'select vectors from a list so that the sum of the vectors gets you from the start to the target', converting between representations ('has magnitude' cards, direction phrases, component form) — 3.7.1's standard-notation work at card level; the follow-ups ask what shape the two equal-sum routes form (the parallelogram law of addition) and whether multiples (including negatives) also reach the target — scalar multiplication and its geometrical interpretation, 3.7.2. Medium: the register is informal (descriptions and diagrams) rather than i-j-k formalism.

resources.title: When are these vectors parallel/perpendicular/the same length?
resources.evidence: The resource classifies vector pairs as 'is parallel to / is perpendicular to / have the same length': the solutions establish parallel iff one is a scalar multiple of the other, perpendicular in 2D iff the gradients multiply to -1, and equal magnitude via Pythagoras on the components — the component notation and magnitude computation of 3.7.1/3.7.3 with the scaling-parallelism geometry of 3.7.2's territory (coded 3.7.1/3.7.3: the classification language — parallel/perpendicular/magnitude — is exactly the notation-and-magnitude core).

resources.title: If $C$ is on this line, can we find the ratio $AC:CB$?
resources.evidence: 'If C is on this line, can we find the ratio AC:CB?' — section division of a line by a point expressed in position vectors; the spec's 3.7.2 text explicitly excepts only the GENERAL ratio theorem while requiring 'understanding that the midpoint of a line segment...' — specific-ratio division of a line by vector addition is the included core.

resources.title: If $ABCDEFGH$ is a regular octagon, what do these vectors add to?
resources.evidence: 'If ABCDEFGH is a regular octagon, what do these vectors add to?' — the well sequences vector sums around a regular polygon (AB + BC + ... chains, diagonals as differences), and the solutions read the resultants off the symmetry ('What can we say about the lines... is parallel to') — vector addition and subtraction interpreted in geometrical terms, 3.7.2 verbatim.

resources.title: If $A$, $P$ and $B$ are collinear, what's the value of $\lambda$?
resources.evidence: 'If A, P and B are collinear, what is the value of lambda?' — the solution writes OP = OL + lambda*LM, expands in the basis {a, b}, and invokes unique decomposition ('any vector in the plane can be written uniquely as') to solve 3*lambda = mu and 1/2 + lambda/2 = mu — collinearity via position vectors (3.7.3) riding vector algebra with geometrical meaning (3.7.2).

resources.title: What is the position vector of $D$ if $ABCD$ is a parallelogram?
resources.evidence: Two-part position-vector exercise: (i) 'What is the position vector of D if ABCD is a parallelogram?' — the parallelogram law AB = DC rearranged for the fourth vertex; (ii) collinearity with a parameter ('The position vectors of points ... are collinear', 'collinear if and only if') — addition/subtraction geometry (3.7.2) and position-vector collinearity reasoning (3.7.3) in one exam-register question. PICK 3.7.2: the purest parallelogram-law exercise in the corpus.

resources.title: What if we join the midpoints of opposite sides of a quadrilateral?
resources.evidence: 'What if we join the midpoints of opposite sides of a quadrilateral?' — the solution computes midpoints as position vectors ((a+b)/2 arithmetic), shows the two joining segments bisect each other — the midpoint understanding 3.7.2 names explicitly ('understanding that the midpoint of a line segment is (a+b)/2'-class work). Medium: no exam-register demand; an exploratory generalisation.

resources.title: Where do $ST$ and $AB$ cross?
resources.evidence: Two-part exam-register question: (i) 'evaluate OM.ON and hence calculate angle MON to the nearest degree' — the scalar product formula and its angle use, 3.7.6 verbatim; (ii) S, T at 2p, 2q with OA = AS (midpoint) and OT = 2TB, then AR = lambda*AB, SR = mu*ST and 'express OR in terms of p and q' twice, solving the two expressions — midpoint/ratio understanding (3.7.2) and the intersection-of-lines lambda/mu technique. PROMOTION: supersedes its stale lane-3-algebra non-overlap row of record (the r8013 precedent — the resource's centre of gravity is vector machinery, not algebra).

resources.title: Can we show the direction of $P'Q'$ is independent of $P$?
resources.evidence: 'Can we show the direction of P'Q' is independent of P?' — an affine-invariance proof by vector arithmetic: P' and Q' defined by the same construction rule from variable P, and P'Q' telescopes to a P-free combination — addition/subtraction of displacement vectors interpreted geometrically (3.7.2). Medium: the target is the invariance, not the operations themselves.

resources.title: Lots of vector lines!
resources.evidence: Twelve lines given ONLY as r = a + mu*b column-vector equations, to be paired by shared properties ('These lines are parallel. These lines are perpendicular. These lines have the same y-intercept...') — the equation of a straight line in vector form r = a + t b (3.7.4) is the raw material, and the pairing includes parallel/perpendicular determination from direction vectors (3.7.5); the teacher notes ask 'Are there any pairs we can match up by just looking at the equations?' — reading direction and position vectors off the vector form. PICK 3.7.4: the purest vector-line-equation material in the corpus.

resources.title: Three lines
resources.evidence: Three lines in 3D given as vector equations a = (4,0,-2) + alpha(-1,1,4) etc.; students predict parallel/perpendicular/intersecting relationships then verify: 'If any two of the lines were parallel, their direction vectors would be the same or related by a scalar multiple'; intersections via 'three equations and two unknowns. If there is a unique solution, then the two lines intersect. If there is no solution they do not' — the skew/intersection determination of 3.7.5 over the r = a + t b form of 3.7.4, with the dot product named for the perpendicularity check. PICK 3.7.5: the corpus's only genuine 3D parallel/skew/intersection Determination exercise.

resources.title: Vector squares
